_comment: The standing accuracy bench. Until #133 this was a convention recorded in prose and nowhere
runnable, so every measurement re-derived its own shell and nothing stopped the next one
quietly using two discs instead of three.
Every entry earns its place by covering something the others cannot. Adding one is cheap --
a bench pass is about a second per track once dumped -- but an entry that duplicates another's
coverage costs attention rather than time, which is the expensive half.
Every sidecar here is a release transcript rather than the disc, and #185 measured what that
is worth: over the 300 cues of Wanda that were read off the images by eye, the sidecar differs
from the disc by 0.1% -- and five of its ten differences are its own lowercase x read as X.
Good enough to rank a change by, and not ground truth. `scripts/truth/` holds the verified
cues and the tools that made them.
kind: 'scored' has a release sidecar and yields CER/WER. 'smoke' does not, and claims no
accuracy at all -- it asserts the pipeline survives the shape of the track. A forced track
scored against a full transcript would report a meaningless number, and reporting one would be
the invented-data failure CLAUDE.md forbids.
A 'scored' entry yields a CUE-LEVEL number only where its cues pair. #229 found King Kong
leaving 529 of 1,704 unpaired -- a Blu-ray extraction against a WEB-DL sidecar -- and reporting
the resulting 21.3% as if it were a read, where the same extraction scores 6.0% with cue
boundaries ignored. run.py refuses the cue-level figure below `PAIRED_ENOUGH` and reports the
track-level one instead, saying which on the row. Every entry now records its unpaired count.
Three of nine entries have now been caught by some version of the same rule -- The Prestige and
Airplane! on convention (#175), King Kong on cut (#229). The bench's own sidecars are the part
of it least likely to have been checked, because nothing fails when they are wrong.

tracks.covers: the tuned baseline; a marked italic act at 6% of characters
the long end (p100 of the library); 18% of lines lean and no sidecar marks one

the third Arial title, and the one whose italic act #123 gains least on. Scored against the SDH sidecar since #175: the track carries 85 bracketed sound cues -- (Door opens), (Ken gasps) -- and the plain sidecar carries none, which was more than half of its measured error. 1,396 cues on both sides exactly.

SDH speaker labels and sound cues, at the best fit of the three SDH tracks (10.5). Smoke rather than scored, and the reason is a bench-design lesson: its track is SDH and its only sidecar is not, so every sound cue is scored against unrelated dialogue. That does not merely inflate its CER -- it puts FALSE entries in the `worse` column, which is the one column this bench tells you to read. Correcting `[CROWD LAUGHlNG]` to `[CROWD LAUGHING]` scored as a regression against a sidecar carrying different text entirely. A scored track needs a sidecar of matching convention, not just any sidecar.

SDH, scored against an SDH sidecar -- and since #229, scored TRACK-LEVEL rather than per cue. The disc is a Blu-ray and the only English sidecar in its folder is a WEB-DL: 1,704 cues against 1,608, and 529 of them pair by start time onto a neighbour's text. That read as 21.3% CER for as long as the bench has existed, and five documents quote the figure as if it described the read. With cue boundaries ignored the same extraction scores 6.0%. #175 taught the bench to check a sidecar's CONVENTION and both sides here are SDH; what nothing checked was the CUT. `PAIRED_ENOUGH` in run.py is the general form.

the all-caps disc, where #134's spacing failure was found. `smoke` since #175 for The Prestige's reason: the track is SDH and renders its sound cues as 72 bracketed lines, and the disc's SDH sidecar renders them as 197 musical notes and one bracket -- two SDH conventions that share almost no characters. Neither sidecar matches, so neither yields a number, and a track that puts false entries in the `worse` column poisons the one figure the bench is read for.

tracks.folder: Once Upon a Time in Mexico (2003) [tmdbid-1428]
tracks.covers: the short and sparse extreme: 106 cues, 2,247 glyphs, forced-subtitle shape. Every per-line median -- the spacing rule, the cap line of #75, the slant estimator of #123 -- needs a population, and nothing else here is small enough to test what happens when there is not one.

the first VOBSUB track on the bench (#140). Every accuracy figure this project had published was PGS -- the decoder for the other codec had shipped and nothing had ever scored it. Plain rather than SDH, and its own disc's SDH sidecar scores the same extraction at 66.4% against this one's 2.5%.

VOBSUB carrying SDH, against the SDH sidecar cut from the same Blu-ray. The disc's other three sidecars score this extraction at 5.0%, 79.7% and 80.7% -- the WEB ones are a different cut -- so it is also the sharpest measurement of what choosing the wrong sidecar costs.
